question.text: Given that $ A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -2 \\ -5 & 6 \end{bmatrix} $ has the LU decomposition $A=LU,$ then $L=$
question.explanation:
To find the matrices $L$ and $U,$ we reduce the matrix $A$ to row echelon form. Whilst doing this, we simultaneously write down the row operations applied to $A$ in terms of matrix multiplication using elementary matrices:

\[ \begin{align*} A &= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -2 \\ -5 & 6 \end{bmatrix} & R_2 &:= R_2 + 5R_1\qquad \Longleftrightarrow \qquad \overbrace{\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 5 & 1 \end{bmatrix}}^{E_1} \cdot A \\[5pt] &\sim \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -2 \\ 0 & -4 \end{bmatrix}\\[5pt] &= U \end{align*}\]

The reduced matrix is upper triangular, so it is our matrix $U.$ Now, since $E_1A=U,$ we can invert $E_1$ to arrive at the desired LU factorization:

\begin{align*} E_1 A &= U \\[5pt] A &= E_1^{-1} U \\[5pt] A &= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 5 & 1 \end{bmatrix}^{-1} U \\[5pt] A &= \underbrace{ \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ -5 & 1 \end{bmatrix} }_{L} \underbrace{ \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -2 \\ 0 & -4 \end{bmatrix} }_{U} \end{align*}

question.explanation:
To find the matrices $L$ and $U,$ we reduce the matrix $A$ to row echelon form. Whilst doing this, we simultaneously write down the row operations applied to $A$ in terms of matrix multiplication using elementary matrices:

\[ \begin{align*} A &= \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -3 \\ 8 & -12 \end{bmatrix} & R_2 &:= R_2 + (-4)R_1\qquad \Longleftrightarrow \quad \overbrace{\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ -4& 1 \end{bmatrix}}^{E_1} \cdot A \\[5pt] &\sim \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -3 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\\[5pt] & = U \end{align*}\]

The reduced matrix is upper triangular, so it is our matrix $U.$ Now, since $E_1A=U,$ we can invert $E_1$ to arrive at the desired LU factorization:

\begin{align*} E_1 A&= U \\[5pt] A &= E_1^{-1} U \\[5pt] A &= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\-4& 1 \end{bmatrix}^{-1} U \\[5pt] A&= \underbrace{ \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 4& 1 \end{bmatrix} }_{L} \underbrace{ \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -3 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} }_{U}. \end{align*}

Therefore, $l_{21}=4,u_{22}=0,$ and $l_{21}+u_{22}=4.$

question.text: Given that $ A = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & -6 \\ -2 & 4 \end{bmatrix} $ has the LU decomposition $A=LU$, then $l_{21}+u_{22}=$
question.explanation:
To find the matrices $L$ and $U,$ we reduce the matrix $A$ to row echelon form. Whilst doing this, we simultaneously write down the row operations applied to $A$ in terms of matrix multiplication using elementary matrices:

\[ \begin{align*} A &= \begin{bmatrix} 3 & -6 \\ -2 & 4 \end{bmatrix} & R_2 &:= R_2 + \left(\dfrac{2}{3}\right)R_1\qquad \Longleftrightarrow \qquad \overbrace{\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ \dfrac{2}{3} & 1 \end{bmatrix}}^{E_1} \cdot A \\[5pt] &\sim \begin{bmatrix} 3 & -6 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\\[5pt] &= U \end{align*}\]

The reduced matrix is upper triangular, so it is our matrix $U.$ Now, since $E_1A=U,$ we can invert $E_1$ to arrive at the desired LU factorization:

\begin{align*} E_1 A &= U \\[5pt] A &= E_1^{-1} U \\[5pt] A &= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ \dfrac 2 3 & 1 \end{bmatrix}^{-1} U \\[5pt] A &= \underbrace{ \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ -\dfrac 2 3 & 1 \end{bmatrix} }_{L} \underbrace{ \begin{bmatrix} 3 & -6 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} }_{U} \end{align*}

Therefore, $l_{21}=-\dfrac 2 3,$ $u_{22}=0,$ and $l_{21}+u_{22}=-\dfrac 2 3.$
